title: Sagas & Distributed Transactions
summary: One action, several services, several databases: how to keep it all-or-nothing without one big transaction.

goals.text: Why one transaction can’t span services
Two-phase commit and why it blocks

steps.title: One trip, three databases
body: A traveller books a trip: a flight, a hotel and a rental car. Each lives in a different service with its own database (database per service, from the previous lessons).
The trip service books the flight — done. The hotel — done. The car — no cars left. Now the traveller has a flight and a hotel they can’t use, and has been charged for both.

callout.text: BEGIN … COMMIT only works inside one database. Across services, there is no built-in “undo everything”.

steps.title: Two-phase commit
body: A classic fix is two-phase commit (2PC). Phase 1: a coordinator asks every participant to prepare — do the work, lock the rows, and promise it can commit (the pings). Phase 2: if all said yes, it tells everyone to commit; if anyone said no, everyone rolls back.
The car service votes no, so nothing is booked anywhere. All or nothing.

callout.text: 2PC is used inside some databases and with XA transactions. It needs every participant to support it — most web APIs and many NoSQL stores don’t.

changes: + Prepare → vote → commit or roll back

tags.text: votes: yes · yes · no → roll back

steps.title: When the coordinator dies
body: The weakness: after preparing, participants must wait for the coordinator’s decision. If it crashes right then, flights and hotels sit “prepared”, holding locks on seats and rooms, unable to commit or roll back on their own.
Other travellers trying to book those seats and rooms wait too — until the coordinator recovers. (The trip itself stays all-or-nothing; it just can’t finish.)

callout.text: 2PC is a blocking protocol: one slow or dead coordinator can freeze every participant. Across services and the internet, that’s usually unacceptable.

steps.title: A saga: commit step by step, undo on failure
body: A saga splits the trip into local transactions that each commit immediately: book flight, then book hotel, then rent car. Nothing is held open.
Every step has a compensating action that semantically undoes it. When the car fails, the saga runs them in reverse: cancel the hotel, then cancel the flight (the red rings).

callout.text: A saga trades isolation for availability: no locks are held across services, but the system is briefly in between states.

steps.title: Orchestration: one service runs the saga
body: In an orchestrated saga, one component — the orchestrator — is a small state machine: it tells each service what to do next, waits for the answer, and decides whether to continue or compensate.
It saves every state change to its own database, so if it crashes it resumes exactly where it stopped.

callout.text: Workflow engines such as Temporal, AWS Step Functions and Camunda are built for this: durable, resumable, observable sagas.

changes: + Saga state saved after every step

steps.title: Choreography: services react to events
body: In a choreographed saga there is no conductor. Flights publishes FlightBooked; Hotels listens, books a room and publishes HotelBooked; Cars listens and rents a car — or publishes CarFailed, which Hotels and Flights react to by cancelling.
No central component to build or run — but the flow is spread across every service, and harder to follow and change.

callout.text: Choreography suits short sagas with few steps. As sagas grow, an orchestrator is usually easier to reason about.

changes: ~ Each service reacts to the previous step’s event

steps.title: The catch: no isolation
body: While a saga runs, other people can see its half-done state: the seat is taken, the hotel isn’t booked yet. And some steps can’t really be undone — an email “your flight is confirmed” has already gone out.
Design for it: use pending states (“reserved”, not “confirmed”), put the step most likely to fail first, and the hardest to undo — charging the card, sending emails — last.

callout.text: A compensation is a new action, not a rollback. A refund is not the same as never having charged.

card.title: Order the steps
lines: 1. check car    likely to fail → first
3. charge card   hard to undo → last

steps.title: Case: crash and resume
body: The orchestrator crashes right after Hotels booked a room — but before it saved that fact. On restart it sees “hotel: pending” and sends the booking request again.
If Hotels books a second room, the traveller pays twice. So every step carries an idempotency key (the saga id + step), and Hotels returns the existing booking instead of creating another.

callout.text: Sagas are at-least-once by nature. Every step and every compensation must be safe to repeat.

steps.title: Case: the undo itself fails
body: The car can’t be rented, so the saga cancels the hotel — but the hotel’s API is down. Giving up isn’t an option: the traveller would be charged for a room they can’t use.
So compensations are retried with backoff until they succeed, and must be safe to repeat. A compensation still stuck after a few hours goes to a queue for a person to resolve.

callout.text: A compensation must be able to succeed eventually. Never design one that can legitimately fail — and alert when one is stuck.

steps.title: Case: a timeout means “unknown”
body: The call to rent the car times out. Did the car service book it before the connection dropped, or not? A timeout is not a failure — the outcome is unknown.

Compensating blindly could cancel a booking that never existed, or leave one that did. Instead, ask: query the car service for request 81-car, or simply retry with the same idempotency key and get the real answer.

callout.text: Treat every remote step as having three outcomes: succeeded, failed, unknown. Only the first two let the saga move on.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A database transaction can’t span several services.
  • Two-phase commit is all-or-nothing but blocks when the coordinator fails.
  • A saga commits step by step and runs compensations on failure.
  • Orchestrate or choreograph; make every step idempotent.
  • Compensations must eventually succeed; a timeout means unknown, not failed.
